chunks.text: Pritchardia pacifica, the Fiji fan palm (also called piu), is a solitary-trunked palm growing to about 15 m with 20-30 large, stiff, fan-shaped leaves roughly 1.2 m across. Its native range is usually given as Tonga, with Wikipedia noting that its populations in Fiji, Samoa, northeastern India (Arunachal Pradesh) and the Marquesas are likely the result of human introduction rather than natural occurrence — an important caveat given how strongly the species is culturally associated with Fiji specifically. The IUCN Red List classifies it as Extinct in the Wild, though other databases disagree and list its status as Not Evaluated, so the conservation picture is genuinely unsettled across sources. In traditional Fijian society its fan-shaped leaves were fashioned into fans called iri masei or ai viu and were reserved exclusively for chiefs, serving the dual purpose of sunshade and, held overhead, rain protection; because a single tree supplied enough leaves for a chief's needs, villages typically kept only one or two specimens. In Arunachal Pradesh, by contrast, local tribal communities use its leaves for thatched roofing — a far more utilitarian, non-status-linked application of the same material.

chunks.source: National Tropical Botanical Garden — Plant Database (Pritchardia pacifica)
chunks.text: The National Tropical Botanical Garden's database gives a close botanical description: a tree to about 10 m with a single stem up to 30 cm thick, fan-shaped leaf blades to a metre long with 73-90 segments pleated at the base, and small yellow-green bisexual flowers (three sepals, three petals) producing round, dark-brown, roughly 12 mm fruits with a single seed. It places the species' native range in Tonga while noting its presence in Fiji, Samoa and the Marquesas is probably introduced, and highlights a wider point of context often missing from popular accounts: the genus Pritchardia comprises about 26 Pacific species, of which 23 are endemic to Hawai'i alone and found nowhere else on Earth — making P. pacifica something of an outlier within its own genus in actually being widespread beyond Hawaii. The database separately confirms the traditional Fijian chiefly-fan use (iri masei/ai viu) described elsewhere, and flags a practical modern concern: the species is a known host for Lethal Yellowing disease, a serious coconut-palm pathogen, and several US states (Louisiana, Texas, Mississippi) accordingly restrict its transport from affected regions.
